text: Why should a `switch` over an enum usually omit its `default` clause?
choices: Without `default`, adding a constant turns every incomplete switch into a compile error that lists the places to update.
A `default` clause on an enum switch is a compile error, because the set is already closed.
Omitting `default` allows the switch to return null for unhandled constants rather than throwing.
Without `default`, the JVM can compile the switch to a jump table instead of a chain of comparisons.
explanation: The compiler knows the set is closed and can verify that every constant is covered. That check is the entire payoff of using an enum instead of `int` constants. Writing `default` tells the compiler you have handled everything, so it stops checking, and a fourth constant then compiles fine and misbehaves at run time in whichever branch you forgot.
